title: Chapter 1 - The hesitation of facing Death
description:
At first, we just wanted to know more about Death. So we went to the City Funeral Home (Nhà Tang lễ Thành phố), hoping to hear the stories of those who work surrounded by Death. But looking at their uneasy faces, perhaps we had been a little too abrupt. Maybe this culture is still not yet ready to talk about death, no matter how familiar with it they are.
We had to emphasize many times that we wanted to hear the story from her perspective, a woman who had worked in funeral services for years, but she kept brushing it off. "I don't have anything to tell you." "You should ask those people over there," she said, pointing to one of her clients. Death seemed like a bad omen to be hidden and avoided, not something to be examined as a human experience, which is what we were trying to do.

title: Chapter 2 - The language of Death
description:
But the rejection can not stop us. If anything, because this was something so few people dared to think about, we grew even more curious and more committed to our subject. Fortunately, we met Ms. H, a funeral florist, and caught an interesting insight: each flower color at a funeral carries its own meaning, as married people one color and orphanages go with another one. Otherwise, the family orders whatever they wish.

In other words, beyond gratitude and filial devotion, flowers are a tender announcement to tell the community who this person was, and where they stood among the living. And so, from the very first petal, Death is no longer the sole property of the one who has gone. It becomes a shared space of ritual, belonging to those who remain.

We realized that in a culture as deeply collective as Vietnam, so long rooted in village ties and communal bonds, it would be an oversight to approach Death as a solitary journey. From this moment, we decided to look at Death through the lens of the funeral, a thread powerfully connecting the one who has left with their family and community.

title: Chapter 3 - Sacred connections 1 - A funeral at home
description:
At Vietnamese funerals, there is always noise and always crowds. Those who come to pay their respects bow before the departed, the family bows back, and this process would last for many days. In those exchanged gestures of reverence, an invisible thread is woven between souls.

At my grandfather's funeral, nestled among the layered mountains of Quảng Trị, in the central part of the country, the mourners included people who had never met him, or perhaps only once or twice, the family of in-laws, the friends of someone in the house. I found myself wondering: who had they come for?

Yet their presence was a quiet affirmation that our family would not grieve alone. And so, in the way that only death can, my grandfather's passing became something unexpectedly tender, a space where we were drawn closer together, and held more firmly than before.
